name: Command a companion
summary: The unit is a pair: the player's own body and one lasting AI partner, usually an animal, with its own health and its own attack. In most versions the partner stays close, joins a fight by itself and obeys a few short orders on one key: go for that enemy, come back, sometimes stay there or scout ahead. It takes the enemy's attention off its fragile master. In some versions it also heals allies near it, carries its master as a mount or warns of enemies. It is not expendable: once killed it is gone for a long wait, and the master is much weaker until it returns. Unlike launched drones there is one partner (or a fixed pair) for the whole life, normally out at its master's side (the mount version stays hidden until called), and its worth lies in where the player sends it.
counterplay: Kill the companion when it is sent in alone: it stays away for a long time, and its master is much weaker without it.
Or go past it: the animal is the tough half and the master the fragile one, so a unit that can reach the master ends the pair.
Stay out of its leash: a companion fights only near its master, so fight from further away or pull it out of his reach.
Use splash and sustained anti-infantry fire, which hurt both bodies when they stand together and cut the animal down on its way in.
Bring armour: claws and teeth do little to vehicles, which can ignore the animal and run its master down.
Read the tell: a companion on the loose means its master is near, even a hidden one.

other_examples.unit: Gunter von Duisburg and his wolves Nacht and Tag (Saxony)
other_examples.note: A third hero of the same game with a different use for his animals: the two wolves can be sent far ahead to scout, one or both, without putting Gunter at risk, and sent again almost as soon as they are back. In a fight they dart in at soldiers from odd angles and vanish again, so they are hard to focus, but they join in only once Gunter himself is close to the enemy, and they can be shot while they are out scouting.

sources.title: Gunter von Duisburg, Iron Harvest Wiki

other_examples.note: A ranged hero who spends the whole match beside a bear with a large health pool of her own; the player has to handle both bodies. One key sends her at a chosen enemy or to a spot to wait there; pointing it at Rexxar calls her back at a run, and pointing it at her makes her hold. Other keys heal her, make her charge and stun, or raise her damage for a while. The page counts him as very weak once she is dead.

sources.title: Rexxar, Heroes of the Storm Wiki
Data:Rexxar (ability data), Heroes of the Storm Wiki

other_examples.unit: Lone Druid and the Spirit Bear
other_examples.note: The bear stays until it is killed, has its own health and can carry and use items like a second hero. It is leashed: too far from the druid it can't attack, unless he owns a late-game item. If it dies the druid loses a fifth of his own maximum health, and after it takes damage from a player it can't be called again for a few seconds.

shooter_analogues.note: A shooter class built on this: the chosen pet trails the player and attacks enemies by itself until it dies, then comes back by itself after a cooldown. Holding the skill key orders a special attack that differs by pet, and each pet also gives its master a small standing bonus such as speed, health regeneration or damage. One skill can bring a downed pet back early at part health, for a longer cooldown.

A dog earned mid-life that stays until it is killed or the match ends. It keeps to its owner's side, growls or whines when enemies are near, runs down anyone who gets close, and hunts the player who kills its owner across the whole map. It is tougher than a player, and the page finds it hard to keep at heel because it keeps chasing; its counters are distance, shotguns and big magazines.

sources.title: Guard Dog, Call of Duty Wiki

shooter_analogues.unit: Guns for Hire and Fangs for Hire
shooter_analogues.note: The player travels with one hired companion (two with a perk, one in co-op), human or animal, and can order it to attack a chosen target or move to a spot; while the player is undetected it tries a silent kill first. A companion that is badly hurt is out of play for a long timer. The dog among them marks enemy positions for the player.

sources.title: Guns for Hire (also Fangs for Hire), Far Cry Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: A helper version for a player with no teammates: a drone follows the lone player, fights, digs and lights up caves, comes over when called with the shout key, takes mining and digging jobs from a laser pointer, and picks its owner up when they go down. Enemies never target it and hazards don't affect it, and it leaves as soon as a second player joins.

player_translation.summary: You are a fragile specialist with an AI animal at your side. It follows you and attacks whatever attacks you, and one key gives it orders: point at an enemy to send it, point at yourself to call it back. It has its own health bar, and if it dies you fight alone until it returns after a long wait.
as_user: You play two bodies with one hand: you aim and fire your own weapon while the companion looks after itself, and your skill is the timing of 'go' and 'come back'.
You send it to hold an enemy's attention while you shoot or slip away, and you call it back before it dies, because losing it costs you most of your strength for a long time.
You watch two health bars and the distance between you: a companion too far from you stops fighting.
Depending on the twist it also heals teammates near it, carries you across open ground until you attack, or runs ahead to look.
as_target: You see an AI animal in its owner's colour with a small health bar of its own coming at you, and you choose: kill it, kite it out of its leash, or go through to the owner.
It fights up close, so distance and armour blunt it; inside a vehicle you can ignore it.
A companion without its owner in view means the owner is near, and a dead companion puts a timer on the owner's nameplate: that is the moment to push.
teammates: The companion holds a target still for the team: a bear on an enemy gunner gives teammates a free shot.
In the healing twist the owner parks the animal beside hurt teammates; in the scouting twist the team sees what the animal sees.
Medics can heal the companion like a soldier, which shortens the time the owner spends alone.
The enemy team calls out 'kill the bear' or 'ignore the bear' and commits together; a split answer feeds the pair.
controls: Q is the companion key, one counted key: with an enemy under the cursor it means attack that one; with open ground under the cursor, go there and wait; with the cursor on yourself, come back at a run.
Its usual behaviour needs no key: it follows, keeps out of your line of fire and fights back when you are attacked.
The mount twist uses the same key on the animal itself: you climb on, move at its speed, and firing drops you off.
The universal keys are unchanged; when you enter a vehicle the companion waits beside it.
feedback: The companion wears its owner's team colour and a marker that only AI bodies have, so nobody takes it for a player.
It has a small health bar of its own; it roars when sent, loud enough for the target to hear, and the owner whistles when calling it back.
The owner's HUD shows its portrait, health and state (following, attacking, returning, or down with a timer) and a faint ring for the leash.
When it dies both teams hear it, and the owner's nameplate shows a small timer until it returns.
changes_from_rts: In an RTS or a MOBA the companion is a second unit to select and steer. With one hand on movement and one on the mouse, every order has to fit on one key that reads what is under the cursor.
It needs dependable AI: paths around cover, staying out of its owner's shots, breaking off when hopeless. A leash keeps its mistakes small.
A top-down shooter has to mark AI bodies clearly as not being players.
In the source the bear went on fighting after Anna was knocked out, and the developers cut his health because of it. Here the companion leaves a few seconds after its owner dies.
The source's wait after a companion's death is long and its length is not given. A player needs the timer on screen, and perhaps a way to shorten it at base.
Its kills count for the owner, and killing it pays the enemy only a little, so sending it in is not feeding.
Every companion is one more AI body for the server and the browser to run, so a match may need a cap on how many such units a team fields.

team_play.notes: The companion pins or distracts a target so that the owner and teammates can shoot it. The healing twist turns it into a walking aid post for nearby teammates, and the scouting twist shares what the animals see. Enemies have to agree whether to kill the animal or go past it.

notes: An AI body per player with path-finding, target choice, a leash and order handling, simulated on the server and shown smoothly in the browser.
It has its own health, hit detection, respawn timer and animations, usually for a four-legged body.
It must not block its owner, teammates or doorways, and must cope with vehicles, water and height.
The mount twist adds a riding state with its own speed and health, and a dismount on attack.
With many players, each companion adds to the count of moving bodies the game must run and draw.
Two bodies for one price: more total health and a second source of damage, plus body-blocking; the owner has to be clearly weaker than a solo unit of the same tier.
If the AI is too good the unit plays itself; if it is too poor the companion feeds. The leash and the recall order are the tuning tools.
A long wait after its death makes the owner dull to play; a short one makes the companion disposable. The developers of the source game cut the bear's health twice in patches.
A companion that heals without a key and can't be told to stop is free healing; keep it slow or out of combat only.
From above, players must tell an AI animal from a player at a glance, and see whose it is.
Two health bars, a leash and a respawn state per pair are a lot to show in a crowded fight.
A companion that hides until needed, as the tiger does, has to appear with a clear cue.

variants.name: Brawler at your side
variants.summary: A tough melee animal follows the master, charges whatever the pair is fighting and takes attack and come-back orders; killed, it returns after a long wait.
variants.seen_in: Iron Harvest Anna Kos and Wojtek; Heroes of the Storm Rexxar and Misha; Borderlands 3 FL4K

variants.name: Healer at your side
variants.summary: The companion also slowly heals friendly soldiers near it and walks over to wounded ones, so where the master leaves it matters to the team.

variants.name: Mount on call
variants.summary: The companion waits out of sight; called, it carries its master, faster and tougher but unable to hide or shoot. Attacking drops the master off and the animal fights beside them for a short time before slipping away.
variants.seen_in: Iron Harvest Olga Morozova and Changa

variants.name: Scouting pair
variants.summary: Two smaller animals that can be sent far ahead to look, and sent again as soon as they are back; they attack only once the master is close to the enemy and are hard to focus.
variants.seen_in: Iron Harvest Gunter and his wolves

variants.name: Helper machine
variants.summary: A small machine in place of an animal: it does chores and little damage, enemies don't target it, and it picks its owner up once when they go down.

variants.name: Leashed twin
variants.summary: The companion is nearly a second fighter with its own gear, but it can't attack beyond a set distance from its master, and its death costs the master a share of their own health.

adds_weaknesses.why: The companion can't fight beyond its leash, and when it dies its master loses a share of their own health as well as their partner.

variants.name: Earned guardian
variants.summary: The companion is a reward earned during a life: it then guards its owner, warns when enemies are near, and goes after whoever kills them.
variants.seen_in: The Guard Dog reward in Call of Duty: Ghosts

adds_strengths.why: Fights as two bodies: the companion takes the enemy's attention and holds targets while its master shoots from safety.

adds_weaknesses.why: Loses most of its strength for a long time when the companion dies, and the master alone is fragile.

counters.why: The companion runs soldiers down and keeps them busy while its master picks them off.

countered_by.why: Splash hurts master and companion together whenever they stand close.
Sustained anti-infantry fire cuts the animal down before it reaches its target.
Claws and teeth barely mark armour, so a vehicle can ignore the companion and go for its master.

open_questions: When the master dies, does the companion vanish, fight on for a moment or go after the killer? (Recommended: it leaves after a few seconds. The source game had to weaken a bear that fought on, and the Call of Duty dog that avenges its owner is hard to control.)
How many AI bodies can a large browser match afford? Should units with a companion be limited in number per team?
Can teammates heal the companion, and does it count as a soldier for healing and for crushing?
How long is the wait after it dies, and can going back to base shorten it?
Does killing a companion pay a reward? (Recommended: a small one.)
Could a second player take the companion's seat, turning the pair into a two-player unit?

The fill agents noted that reinforce-squad's respawning-followers twist matches only the companion's return after a wait. Should a unit with a companion link both patterns, or is the return part of this one? (Recommended: part of this one.)

shooter_fit.reason: Pets already work in shooters (pet classes, guard dogs, hired animals) and give a fragile specialist a front line, but each companion is an AI body to simulate, send over the network and tell apart from players in a top-down browser game.
